Behemoth

/bih-HEE-muhth/ - the stress falls on HEE · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Behemoth means something of tremendous power or size.

The quarry's new excavator was a behemoth, its bucket big enough to cradle a school bus and its treads taller than the foreman.

Worked Example

The city's new stadium rose like a behemoth over the rowhouses of the old neighborhood: ninety thousand seats, parking for a small city of cars, and lights that turned midnight into noon for three blocks in every direction.

Behemoth says more than 'huge': borrowed from the name of a monstrous beast, it carries a shudder — a thing so big it overwhelms everything near it, often with a hint that such size is more menacing than admirable.

How Behemoth Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

giant

giant: anything unusually large, with none of behemoth's monstrous shadow

juggernaut

juggernaut: a huge force that also moves, crushing whatever stands in its path

Antonyms

runt

runt: the smallest and weakest of a group

lightweight

lightweight: something too small or slight to carry much force

How Strong Is It? — giant → behemoth → juggernaut

giant vs. behemoth

giant vs. behemoth: Giant simply reports unusual size — a giant pumpkin is a happy thing — while behemoth adds monstrous scale and a note of dread.

juggernaut vs. behemoth

juggernaut vs. behemoth: A juggernaut goes beyond a behemoth: a behemoth overwhelms just by standing there, while a juggernaut is in motion, rolling over rivals and roadblocks alike.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — behemoth

Root — behemoth: a great beast (Hebrew behemot)

Put it together

Put it together: Behemoth resists dissection: English took it whole from Hebrew behemot, the great grass-eating beast described in the Book of Job — a creature so vast no hunter could take it. There is nothing to peel off here; the word is the monster's own name, lent ever since to anything of monstrous size.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Behemoth is a whole-word borrowing from Hebrew, the name of the giant beast in the Book of Job. Its root built no other English word, so there is no relative to spot — remember it as a monster's proper name that became a common noun.

Strength Check

Word Choice

vivid / journalistic

Reach for behemoth when size alone is the story and you want a shiver in it — a behemoth of a corporation, a behemoth truck. Its unit-mate colossus is grand and statuesque, a marvel to look up at; a behemoth looms and crowds. For a big force on the move, juggernaut adds the momentum.
